questions.stem: INDIRA GANDHI nationalised India's major banks in the year:
questions.explanation: 19 July 1969 — Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 major private banks with deposits ≥ ₹50 crore. Another 6 banks nationalised in 1980. Total 20 nationalised banks + SBI (nationalised 1955, separately). Narasimha Committee (1991) recommended consolidation; PSU-bank mergers accelerated 2019-20 (PNB+OBC+United Bank etc.).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The STATE BANK OF INDIA was formed by nationalising:

options.option_text: Imperial Bank of India (1955)
Bank of England
Reserve Bank of India
Punjab National Bank

questions.explanation: SBI Act 1955 — Imperial Bank of India (formed 1921 merger of three presidency banks) was nationalised as SBI on 1 July 1955. Oldest commercial bank in India (ancestry traces to Bank of Calcutta, 1806). Currently India's largest bank by assets.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's FIRST bank (still operational in some form) was:

options.option_text: Bank of Calcutta (1806, later Bank of Bengal, Imperial Bank, SBI)
Allahabad Bank (1865)

questions.explanation: Bank of Calcutta — 1806, first presidency bank. Later became Bank of Bengal (1809), one of the three presidency banks (Bengal, Bombay, Madras) merged in 1921 to form Imperial Bank of India, which in turn became SBI in 1955. Allahabad Bank (1865) is the oldest continuing JOINT-STOCK bank founded by Indians; merged with Indian Bank in 2020.

questions.stem: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was set up in:
questions.explanation: NABARD — est. 12 July 1982 by NABARD Act, 1981. Apex development financial institution for rural / agricultural credit. HQ: Mumbai. Took over agricultural refinance from RBI + credit roles from various bodies.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: PRIORITY SECTOR LENDING (PSL) target for scheduled commercial banks is:

options.option_text: 20% of ANBC
40% of ANBC

questions.explanation: RBI mandate: 40% of ANBC (or credit-equivalent of off-balance-sheet exposures, whichever higher) to priority sectors. PSL includes agriculture (18%), MSMEs, education, housing, export credit, social infrastructure. Failure to meet target — banks deposit the shortfall in RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund). Adjusted Net Bank Credit.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The SECOND nationalisation of Indian banks (1980) included how many banks?
questions.explanation: 6 more banks nationalised on 15 April 1980: Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, Vijaya Bank. Combined with 1969 nationalisation (14 banks), total 20 PSU banks. Several have since been merged or with SBI associate banks (2017).

questions.stem: The DEPOSIT INSURANCE cover in India (up to) is held by:

options.option_text: SEBI
DICGC
NABARD
Finance Ministry directly

questions.explanation: DICGC — est. 1978 merger (Deposit Insurance Corp. + Credit Guarantee Corp. of India). RBI subsidiary. Insures each depositor up to ₹5 lakh per bank (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020). Covers savings, FD, RD, current accounts. Premium paid by banks. Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, subsidiary of RBI.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India, originally established as a private shareholders' bank, was nationalised in which year?

options.option_text: 1935 — year the Reserve Bank commenced operations
1947 — year India gained its political independence
1948 — a year after Indian Independence was declared
1949 — under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act

questions.explanation: RBI was established on 1 April 1935 as a privately-owned institution under the RBI Act, 1934. It was nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. Option A (1935) is the most common distractor — that is the year of establishment, not nationalisation.

questions.stem: The first Regional Rural Bank (RRB) to be set up in India was?

options.option_text: Baroda Rajasthan Kshetriya Gramin Bank, Rajasthan
Prathama Bank, sponsored by Syndicate Bank, Uttar Pradesh
Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas Bank, Andhra Pradesh
Krishna Grameena Bank, sponsored by Canara Bank, Karnataka

questions.explanation: Prathama Bank was inaugurated on 2 October 1975 in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh, sponsored by Syndicate Bank — it was the very first RRB under the RRB Act, 1976. The others are genuine RRBs but were established subsequently. Candidates often confuse the sponsor bank (Syndicate Bank, not SBI) as another trap.

questions.stem: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) was formed in 1978 by merging which two earlier bodies?

options.option_text: Deposit Insurance Corporation and Credit Guarantee Corporation of India
Reserve Bank Guarantee Fund and Agricultural Credit Corporation Ltd
Export Credit Guarantee Corporation and Industrial Finance Corporation
State Bank Guarantee Fund and National Credit Corporation of India

questions.explanation: Deposit Insurance Corporation (DIC) was set up in 1962 to insure bank deposits, and Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd (CGCI) was set up in 1971 to guarantee loans to small borrowers. They were merged in July 1978 to form DICGC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of RBI. The other options name real financial bodies but played no role in DICGC's formation.

questions.stem: The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, providing a grievance-redressal mechanism for bank customers, was first introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in which year?

options.option_text: 1991 — coinciding with the Narasimham Committee reforms
1995 — as the first banking consumer redressal scheme
2002 — when the scheme received its first major revision
2006 — when the scheme was significantly expanded again

questions.explanation: RBI introduced the Banking Ombudsman Scheme in 1995 under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. It was substantially revised in 2002 and again in 2006 (widening the grounds for complaints) — these revision years are common distractors. 1991 is wrong; the Narasimham Committee dealt with structural reforms, not consumer grievances.

questions.stem: The concept of differentiated bank licences, which gave rise to Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks in India, was formally recommended by which committee?

options.option_text: Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion, 2008 report
Nachiket Mor Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services, 2014
Y.H. Malegam Committee on Microfinance Institutions, 2011
Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms, 2009

questions.explanation: The Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low Income Households chaired by Nachiket Mor (2013–14) recommended differentiated or 'niche' banking licences including Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks. RBI issued guidelines for both in 2014–15. Option D (Rajan Committee, 2009) addressed broader financial sector reform but predated the SFB/PB framework.

questions.stem: The Imperial Bank of India (1921) was formed by amalgamating three Presidency Banks. Which of the following was NOT one of the three constituent banks?

options.option_text: Bank of Bengal, established in Calcutta in 1806
Bank of Bombay, established in Bombay in 1840
Bank of Madras, established in Madras in 1843
Bank of Punjab, established in Lahore in 1894

questions.explanation: Imperial Bank of India (1921) arose from the merger of the three Presidency Banks — Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840), and Bank of Madras (1843). Bank of Punjab (founded 1894, Lahore) was a separate joint-stock bank with no role in this merger. Imperial Bank was later converted into State Bank of India in 1955. Candidates frequently guess Bank of Madras as the 'odd one out' because it was the last to be established.

questions.stem: Under which section of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, is the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) requirement prescribed for scheduled commercial banks?

options.option_text: Section 24 — governs the Statutory Liquidity Ratio requirements
Section 42 — applicable to all banks listed in the Second Schedule
Section 17 — covers the general business of the Reserve Bank
Section 49 — governs the Bank Rate determination mechanism

questions.explanation: Section 42(1) of the RBI Act, 1934 mandates every scheduled bank (listed in the Second Schedule) to maintain a Cash Reserve Ratio with the RBI. Option A is the most tempting trap: Section 24 does deal with reserves, but it is Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — governing SLR, not CRR. Section 49 of the RBI Act covers the Bank Rate; Section 17 covers the permissible business of RBI itself.
